entries.topicDescription: Functions that execute a block of code within the context of an object.

tips.title: let — transform nullable values
tips.content:
'let' executes a block only when the object is non-null (when used with ?.).
The object is referenced as 'it' inside the block.
Returns the result of the block.

Best used for: executing code with a non-null value, 
transforming an object into something else, 
or limiting variable scope.

tips.title: apply — configure an object
tips.content:
'apply' executes a block where 'this' refers to the object.
Returns the object itself (not the block result).

Perfect for object configuration — setting multiple properties 
on a newly created object without repeating the variable name.

Think of it as: "apply these settings to this object, then give it back."

tips.title: also — side effects without changing the chain
tips.content:
'also' executes a block (referencing the object as 'it') 
and returns the original object unchanged.

Use it for side effects: logging, validation, or debugging 
in the middle of a call chain without breaking the flow.

Think of it as: "and also do this."

tips.title: run turns a block into an expression that returns its result
tips.content:
run takes a lambda and returns whatever the last expression evaluates to. As an extension (obj.run { }) the object becomes 'this' inside the block, so it is a good fit when you want to call several members of an object and compute a result from them.

There is also a form with no receiver, run { }, that just gives you a scope: local variables declared inside stay inside, and the block's last expression becomes the value. That makes it handy for a multi-step initialization of a val.

tips.title: with calls several members of one object without repeating its name
tips.content:
with(obj) { } is not an extension function: you pass the object as an argument, and inside the block it is 'this'. It returns the result of the last expression, like run. It reads best when you already have a non-null object and want to read or set many of its members.

If the value can be null, prefer obj?.run { } (or let), because with has no safe-call form.

tips.title: takeIf and takeUnless turn a condition into a nullable value
tips.content:
takeIf { predicate } returns the receiver if the predicate is true and null otherwise; takeUnless is the opposite. Combined with the safe call and the Elvis operator they let you express "use this value only if it is valid" in one expression instead of an if statement and a temporary.

Use them for validation-like checks on a value you are already holding. If the condition becomes long or has side effects, a normal if is clearer.

tips.title: x?.let { } ?: default is not an if/else
tips.content:
The pattern user?.let { ... } ?: fallback looks like "if user is not null do this, else that". It isn't: the Elvis operator runs the fallback whenever the whole left side evaluates to null, and that includes the case where user is non-null but the let block itself returns null.

It works as an if/else only when the block can never return null. When the block returns a nullable value, or has a branch that returns null, you get the fallback in the "wrong" case. Use a real if/else when you mean if/else.

tips.title: Avoid deeply nested scope functions — this and it get ambiguous
tips.content:
Scope functions are easy to stack, but each level changes what 'this' or 'it' means. Inside a nested let, 'it' is the inner value and the outer 'it' is hidden; inside nested lambdas with receiver, 'this' is the innermost receiver and the outer one is only reachable through a label. Readers (and you, later) have to work out which object a name refers to.

Give the parameter a name when you nest (let { user -> ... }), keep nesting to one level, and extract a function when a block gets long.

tips.title: Sometimes a plain local variable is better than a scope function
tips.content:
A scope function is worth it when it removes repetition or limits a variable's scope. Wrapping a single statement in let, also or run only adds a lambda and a level of indentation, and it makes the code harder to step through in a debugger.

A useful test: if you can't say what the scope function buys you (a shorter null-check, a scoped temporary, configuring an object in one place), write it without one.
